title: OpenAI parity — lossiness quantifier and compatibility routing policy
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Summary:
Build a compatibility gateway component that (1) computes a per-response "lossiness score" when mapping between Redwood's response model and OpenAI Responses semantics and (2) uses that score to drive routing/fallback policies. The goal is to make migrations and hosted/dedicated/private interop predictable: degrade gracefully, expose clear diagnostics to customers, and automate safe fallbacks when parity loss crosses thresholds.

Why this work matters:
- Customers migrating from OpenAI Responses expect behavioural parity; subtle deltas (structured outputs, toolcall ordering, stream termination events) create customer-facing bugs.
- We need automated, measurable criteria to decide when to route to an alternative model variant, enable a shim transform, or surface a customer-facing warning.

Scope & success criteria:
- Define a lossiness quantifier (LQ) that combines schema mismatch, token-level divergence, toolcall fidelity, and stream-event alignment into a single 0..1 score.
- Implement a lightweight runtime LQ evaluator for the compatibility gateway that runs in the streaming path with bounded CPU overhead (target < 2ms median additional latency).
- Add routing policies based on LQ + SLOs: (a) allow shim transform when 0 < LQ < 0.2, (b) enable alternative parity model variant when 0.2 <= LQ < 0.6, (c) trigger canary rollback and customer alert when LQ >= 0.6 for sustained window.
- Surface telemetry dashboards and per-request diagnostics (lossiness breakdown + example mismatch tokens) in Console.
- Canary plan validated on 10% of new hosted Responses-compatible requests for two weeks with manual QA and automated contract tests.

Design notes & heuristics (high level):
- Components of the LQ: 1) SchemaMismatchRate: fraction of required structured fields missing or typed incorrectly; 2) ToolcallFidelity: count of toolcalls that differ in name/args/order vs expected; 3) StreamBoundaryDelta: probability mass of events (done/err/end_of_stream) misordered or missing; 4) TokenDiffNormalized: normalized edit-distance between expected canonical tokens and observed tokens with special weighting for control tokens (stop, function_call tokens).
- Weighted aggregator: LQ = w1*SchemaMismatchRate + w2*ToolcallFidelity + w3*StreamBoundaryDelta + w4*TokenDiffNormalized. Initial weights: w1=0.4, w2=0.25, w3=0.15, w4=0.2. We will A/B tune weights during the canary.
- Canonical "expected" outputs are derived from a small goldset of prompts we maintain per-model + dynamic ground truth derived from a parity reference run (gold-run) on a trusted model variant.
- To limit CPU cost, use sampling and heuristics: evaluate full LQ for N=1 in-flight request per client per minute; otherwise run lightweight checks (schema hashes and toolcall presence).

Routing policy examples:
- LQ < 0.05: pass-through, no shim.
- 0.05 <= LQ < 0.2: apply non-lossy shim (e.g., field coercions, name mappings) and mark trace with shim=true.
- 0.2 <= LQ < 0.6: route to parity-optimized model variant or higher-precision quantization profile; increment cost meter but prioritize correctness.
- LQ >= 0.6 for 3m rolling window: failover to previously known-good runtime for that customer (if available) and escalate to oncall + send customer-facing advisory.

Telemetry & metrics to ship:
- Per-model LQ histogram (1m rollups) and trendlines.
- Percentage of requests that used shim vs routed to parity model.
- Customer-visible regressions flagged by canary QA harness.
- Per-request lossiness breakdown returned in developer debug responses (for orgs with debug enabled).

Testing & QA:
- Extend existing responses-compat test harness to include: schema-fuzzing, toolcall-order permutations, partial stream truncation, and token-level synthetic drift tests.
- Contract tests: create a set of 500 canonical prompts and expected outputs for each supported model family.
- Canary: 10% of production traffic for 14 days, with rollback gate if weekly LQ median for any customer > 0.35.

Trade-offs considered:
- Latency vs fidelity: per-request full-eval increases latency; mitigated by sampling + lightweight checks.
- Cost: routing to higher-fidelity model variants will increase cost; policy uses economic thresholds (cost per corrected request) to decide.
- Privacy: storing canonical outputs for goldsets must obey customer data policies; goldsets use synthetic and opted-in examples only.

Rollout plan & instrumentation work needed:
1) Implement LQ evaluator library in runtime (C++/Rust) and a JS shim for local testing.
2) Add routing rules into smart router with LQ inputs; ensure deterministic behavior under retries.
3) Console: add LQ dashboards and per-route leakage alerts.
4) Update SDKs to expose developer debug headers for lossiness breakdown.
5) Run canary, collect telemetry, tune weights, then flip policy flags for 50% and 100% after sign-off.
